LESSON 1 • Cause & Consequence / Migration & Settlement

After the Romans Left — Why Did Angles, Saxons & Jutes Settle in Britain? (c. AD 410–600)

Key Enquiry: Who were the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, and why did they cross the North Sea to settle in Britain after AD 410?
[1.1] c. AD 410–500: Crossing the North Sea — Push & Pull Reasons

After Emperor Honorius warned British towns in AD 410 to guard themselves, the last Roman legions marched away forever. Across the stormy North Sea lived seafaring Angles, Saxons, and Jutes. Their homelands lay along low coasts in Jutland, Angeln, and Saxony (modern Denmark and northern Germany). Rising sea tides flooded their soggy marshes, ruining vital grain harvests (push reasons).

Meanwhile, island Britain offered mild weather, rich fertile farmland, and unguarded green river valleys (pull reasons). Whole families packed iron tools, seeds, and livestock into clinker-built wooden rowing boats like the Nydam oak ship. They steered across the waves and up eastern rivers to clear productive new farms.

[1.2] 5th–6th Century AD: Timber Halls, Craftwork & Village Life

Early Anglo-Saxon settlers rarely moved into crumbling Roman stone towns, calling those roofless walls the "work of giants". Instead, free farmers called ceorls built cosy villages beside clear streams, like West Stow in Suffolk. Villagers dug sunken wattle-and-daub workshops topped with steep thatched roofs. Inside, craftspeople wove warm woollen cloaks on upright looms and forged sharp iron tools.

At the heart of each settlement stood a grand rectangular timber mead hall. Around a roaring central hearth fire sat a warrior ruler or cyning (king). He shared roasted meat, sweet honey mead, and gleaming gold rings with loyal fighters while poets sang heroic tales.

[1.3] c. AD 550–650: Seven Kingdoms & Anglo-Saxon Words Today

Gradually, rival warbands joined into seven major kingdoms known as the Heptarchy: Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex. From the Angles came the lasting name Englaland, meaning "land of the Angles" (England), where villagers spoke Old English.

Look closely at any British map today and Anglo-Saxon clues leap right out! Town endings like -ham (Birmingham, village), -ton (Brighton, fenced farm), and -ford (Oxford, river crossing) come straight from Old English. Before becoming Christians, settlers named four weekdays after pagan gods: Tiw (Tuesday), Woden (Wednesday), Thunor (Thursday), and Frige (Friday).

LESSON 2 • Evidential Understanding / Archaeological Inference

Ship Burials & Monasteries — What Do Sutton Hoo & Christian Monks Reveal? (c. AD 597–750)

Key Enquiry: What does the Sutton Hoo ship burial reveal about Anglo-Saxon kings, and how did Christianity change Britain?
[2.1] c. AD 625 & 1939: The Ghost Ship in Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo

In 1939, Suffolk landowner Edith Pretty asked keen local archaeologist Basil Brown to excavate grassy Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo. Acidic sandy soil had completely rotted the oak timbers and human bones away. Yet neat rows of rusted iron rivets still traced a ghostly 27-metre ship dragged uphill from the river around AD 625.

Inside its collapsed wooden burial chamber lay dazzling royal grave goods, probably honouring King Raedwald of East Anglia. Archaeologists uncovered an iconic iron-and-bronze helmet and heavy patterned gold belt buckles. Beside them shone glowing garnet sword fittings traded from India and Sri Lanka, Byzantine silver spoons, and Frankish gold coins.

[2.2] AD 597–635: Two Paths to Christianity — Canterbury & Lindisfarne

Sutton Hoo blended a pagan ship burial with Christian spoons because Britain's religious beliefs were changing fast. In AD 597, Pope Gregory in Rome sent the missionary monk Augustine to Canterbury in Kent. Pagan King Ethelbert was married to Christian Frankish Queen Bertha, who prayed faithfully at ancient St Martin's Church. Ethelbert welcomed Augustine warmly and allowed Britain's first Anglo-Saxon cathedral.

Meanwhile, a second Christian path arrived from the misty north-west. In AD 635, the gentle Irish-Scottish monk Aidan sailed from the island monastery of Iona to Northumbria. Beside Christian King Oswald, Aidan founded a famous coastal priory on Lindisfarne (Holy Island).

[2.3] c. AD 664–731: Monasteries, Illuminated Gospels & Venerable Bede

Soon stone monasteries blossomed across Britain for daily prayer, schooling, and art. High on the cliffs at Whitby, wise Abbess Hilda led a double monastery of monks and nuns. She also hosted the AD 664 Synod of Whitby to unite church customs. Inside quiet scriptoriums, scribes cut feather quills and painted onto smooth calfskin vellum.

Around AD 715, island monks painted the breathtaking Lindisfarne Gospels, twisting animal interlace around Latin scripture. At Jarrow in AD 731, scholar-monk Venerable Bede finished his History of the English Church and People. That landmark book earned his title "Father of English History" and popularised AD dates!

LESSON 3 • Cause & Consequence / Technological Advantage

Fury of the Northmen — Why Did Vikings Raid Lindisfarne & Conquer Kingdoms? (AD 793–878)

Key Enquiry: Why did Viking raiders cross the sea from Scandinavia in AD 793, and how did the Great Heathen Army nearly conquer all England?
[3.1] 8 June AD 793: Dragon Prows Strike Holy Island, Lindisfarne

On 8 June AD 793, sleek wooden warships with carved dragon prows sliced silently onto Holy Island at Lindisfarne. Fierce Viking raiders from Scandinavia (Norway, Denmark, and Sweden) burst into the famous coastal priory. Isolated island monasteries were wealthy soft targets by the sea. Each church held gleaming silver chalices, gold reliquaries, jewelled Gospels, and unarmed monks with no soldiers nearby.

Shockwaves of fear rippled rapidly across Christian Europe. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle recorded "fiery dragons" in the sky before "heathen men miserably destroyed God's church at Lindisfarne". Meanwhile, the Northumbrian scholar Alcuin wept that such terror had never before appeared from the sea.

[3.2] 8th–9th Century AD: Clinker-Built Longships — Engineering Marvels

What gave Viking seafarers such astonishing speed and sudden surprise? Their secret weapon was the clinker-built longship. Master shipwrights overlapped flexible split oak strakes (planks), fastened them with iron rivets, and sealed seams with waterproof tarred wool. Twin steering oars and symmetrical double-pointed ends let crews reverse quickly off narrow beaches.

Across stormy open oceans, crews raised a wide square woollen sail. Whenever winds dropped, warriors lowered the tall mast and pulled long wooden oars. Crucially, a longship's flat hull needed barely a 1-metre shallow draught, gliding straight up shallow English rivers to strike inland towns!

[3.3] AD 865–877: From Summer Raiders to the Great Heathen Army

Back home in mountainous Norway and sandy Denmark, growing families faced a sharp shortage of fertile farmland. Ambitious chieftains also craved silver hoards, trade wealth, and rich new kingdoms of their own. For seventy years, Viking fleets struck quickly in summer and sailed home before winter.

Everything changed in AD 865, when a huge Great Heathen Army landed in eastern England to conquer and settle! Led by brothers Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan alongside warlord Guthrum, the Vikings built fortified winter camps like Repton. They captured York (renamed Jorvik in AD 866) and crushed East Anglia and Mercia, leaving only Wessex unconquered by AD 877!

LESSON 4 • Historical Significance & Leadership

Alfred the Great, Burhs & the Danelaw — How Did Wessex Survive? (AD 871–899)

Key Enquiry: How did King Alfred save Wessex in AD 878, and why do historians call him 'Alfred the Great'?
[4.1] From Athelney Marshes to Victory at Edington (AD 878)

In January AD 878, right after Twelfth Night, Viking leader Guthrum launched a surprise midwinter attack on Chippenham in Wessex. Wessex stood alone as the last unconquered Anglo-Saxon kingdom! Forced to flee, King Alfred hid with a tiny band on misty Athelney deep inside the Somerset marshes. There he sheltered safely while planning a bold spring fightback.

That spring, Alfred rode out to Egbert's Stone, where thousands of loyal Wessex fyrd farmer-warriors cheered his return. In May AD 878, Alfred's tightly locked shield wall smashed Guthrum's army below the hills at the Battle of Edington. The victorious Saxons chased the Vikings back to camp and saved Wessex.

[4.2] Peace with Guthrum & Creating the Danelaw (AD 878–886)

Surrounded and starving inside his fortified camp after Edington, Guthrum finally surrendered. Instead of executing his rival, wise King Alfred stood as godfather when Guthrum was baptised as a Christian named Aethelstan. By AD 886, Alfred also recaptured walled London, styling himself King of the English on silver pennies.

Their famous Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum divided England along the old Roman road called Watling Street. Alfred ruled Anglo-Saxon Wessex and western Mercia in the south and west. Meanwhile, Vikings governed northern and eastern England under Danish law in the Danelaw, where -by and -thorpe villages flourished.

[4.3] Fortified Burhs, Warships & Schools of Learning (AD 880–899)

After winning peace, King Alfred refused to be caught off guard ever again. Across Wessex, he built a clever network of 33 fortified towns called burhs, including Wareham and Wallingford. Giant earth ramparts stood so no village lay over 20 miles from safety, while 60-oar warships patrolled the coasts.

Believing wisdom mattered as much as swords, Alfred founded court schools and translated Latin books into Old English for nobles. He sent crystal reading pointers like the Alfred Jewel to bishops and launched the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Those lasting achievements earned his unique title in British history: Alfred the Great.

LESSON 5 • Similarity, Difference & Challenging Stereotypes

Life in Jorvik & the Danelaw — Were the Vikings Only Fierce Raiders? (c. AD 876–1000)

Key Enquiry: What does archaeology from Jorvik (York) reveal about everyday Viking settlers, traders, and craftworkers?
[5.1] Digging Beneath Coppergate in Jorvik (c. AD 876–950)

Monks who suffered raids described Vikings only as fierce warriors, yet archaeology tells a richer story! Between 1976 and 1981, archaeologists digging beneath Coppergate ("street of the cup-makers") in York uncovered Viking Jorvik. Deep, wet, oxygen-free peat stopped bacteria from rotting buried wood and leather, preserving over 40,000 everyday objects.

Crowded timber workshops lined Jorvik's bustling streets, where skilled craftworkers stitched leather shoes and turned wooden bowls. Families also carved smooth bone ice-skates and counters for the tactical board game hnefatafl. Finely carved deer-antler combs, tweezers, and ear-spoons prove that Viking settlers cared deeply about neat hair and daily hygiene!

[5.2] Global Merchants From Baghdad to the North Atlantic (9th–10th Century AD)

Busy Jorvik soon grew into a wealthy international trading port linking northern Britain to the wider world. Inside Coppergate's dark mud, archaeologists found shimmering silk from Byzantium (Constantinople) and golden Baltic amber. Excavators also unearthed German wine jars and a tropical cowrie shell carried all the way from the Red Sea.

Eastwards, Viking merchants sailed Russian rivers, trading warm furs and walrus ivory for Arabic silver dirham coins from Baghdad and Samarkand. Westwards, daring Norse navigators steered broad cargo ships called knarrs across the icy North Atlantic. Those fearless sailors settled Iceland, Greenland, and Vinland in North America!

[5.3] Families, Thing Law-Assemblies & Old Norse Legacy (9th–11th Century AD)

Across the Danelaw countryside, most settler families lived on peaceful green farms. Free farmers called karls ploughed barley and raised sheep, while enslaved workers called thralls did the hardest labour. Married Viking women held strong legal rights and wore iron household keys on their belts. Wives ran farms while husbands sailed, owned land, and could demand a divorce.

Communities met outdoors at a law-assembly called a Thing, such as Tynwald Hill, to vote on laws and settle disputes. As Norse settlers married Anglo-Saxon neighbours and adopted Christianity, Old Norse gave modern English everyday words. These include sky, window, egg, knife, husband, and Thursday!

LESSON 6 • Change, Continuity & Turning Points

Aethelflaed, Athelstan, Cnut & 1066 — Who Won the Struggle for England? (AD 900–1066)

Key Enquiry: How did Anglo-Saxon and Viking rulers forge one united Kingdom of England — and why did it all change in 1066?
[6.1] Aethelflaed "Lady of the Mercians" & King Athelstan (AD 911–939)

After wise King Alfred died in AD 899, his determined children pushed steadily northwards into the Danelaw. Alfred's bold daughter Aethelflaed, known as the Lady of the Mercians, ruled Mercia from AD 911 to 918. She built fortified burhs at Tamworth and Warwick and led Mercian armies to recapture Viking Derby and Leicester.

Aethelflaed helped raise her nephew Athelstan, who marched north to capture Viking York in AD 927. When northern rulers united against him in AD 937, their armies clashed at the Battle of Brunanburh. Athelstan crushed the giant Viking, Scottish, and Strathclyde alliance, proudly becoming the first true King of All England.

[6.2] Danegeld, King Cnut's North Sea Empire & Edward the Confessor (AD 991–1065)

Yet peaceful rule across united England did not last forever. From AD 991, fresh Danish fleets raided England, so anxious King Aethelred paid vast silver tributes called Danegeld ("Dane-gold"). Still the raiders returned for heavier payments until Danish prince Cnut won the English crown in AD 1016.

King Cnut married Queen Emma and protected English churches and laws. Until AD 1035, he ruled England peacefully alongside Denmark and Norway in a mighty North Sea Empire. Later, gentle Saxon King Edward the Confessor regained the English crown. Near the Thames, he built grand Westminster Abbey, consecrated in December 1065.

[6.3] One Crown, Three Rivals: Stamford Bridge to Hastings (January–October 1066)

When Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, England's royal Witan council crowned powerful Saxon earl Harold Godwinson. Immediately, two rivals claimed the crown: Norwegian Viking King Harald Hardrada and Duke William of Normandy. Harold marched 185 miles north in four days, crushing Hardrada at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.

That northern victory ended the Viking Age, yet Duke William's fleet landed in Sussex just three days later! Footsore after marching 250 miles south, Harold's shield wall fought bravely all day on 14 October 1066 at the Battle of Hastings. At dusk brave Harold fell, and Norman rule began.

CLASSROOM CHECK-FOR-UNDERSTANDING 30 ORAL & EXERCISE-BOOK QUESTIONS

Whole-Unit Knowledge Check (Lessons 1–6)

Please do not write inside this reusable textbook — answer orally with your partner or in your exercise book!

Lesson 1: After the Romans Left — Why Did Angles, Saxons & Jutes Settle in Britain? (c. AD 410–600)
  1. Which three seafaring peoples crossed the North Sea from Jutland, Angeln, and Saxony to settle in Britain after AD 410?
  2. What was a key "push reason" driving families to leave their North Sea coastal homelands in the 5th century?
  3. In an early Anglo-Saxon settlement like West Stow, who was the "cyning" and who were the "ceorls"?
  4. What name do historians give to the seven main Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex)?
  5. Which four modern days of the week are named after the pagan Anglo-Saxon gods Tiw, Woden, Thunor, and Frige?
Lesson 2: Ship Burials & Monasteries — What Do Sutton Hoo & Christian Monks Reveal? (c. AD 597–750)
  1. Even though acidic Suffolk sand rotted the oak wood and bones in Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo, how did Basil Brown prove a 27-metre ship was buried there in 1939?
  2. Where had the glowing red garnets set into Sutton Hoo’s gold shoulder clasps and sword fittings travelled from?
  3. Who arrived at Canterbury in AD 597 from Rome, and who founded Lindisfarne Priory in Northumbria in AD 635?
  4. What smooth material were precious illuminated manuscripts like the Lindisfarne Gospels painted onto using feather quills?
  5. Which scholar-monk at Jarrow completed his famous History of the English Church and People in AD 731, popularising AD dates?
Lesson 3: Fury of the Northmen — Why Did Vikings Raid Lindisfarne & Conquer Kingdoms? (AD 793–878)
  1. Why were coastal monasteries like Lindisfarne (raided on 8 June AD 793) considered tempting "soft targets" by early Viking crews?
  2. How did a clinker-built Viking longship’s "1-metre shallow draught" help warriors attack inland towns?
  3. What natural material soaked in pine tar did Norse shipwrights press between overlapping oak strakes to make longships watertight?
  4. How did Viking attacks change dramatically in AD 865 when the Great Heathen Army landed under Ivar the Boneless, Halfdan, and Guthrum?
  5. After the Great Heathen Army captured York (renaming it Jorvik), East Anglia, and Mercia, which single Anglo-Saxon kingdom remained unconquered by AD 877?
Lesson 4: Alfred the Great, Burhs & the Danelaw — How Did Wessex Survive? (AD 871–899)
  1. Where did King Alfred hide with a small band of followers after Guthrum's surprise Twelfth Night attack on Chippenham in January AD 878?
  2. At which May AD 878 battle in Wiltshire did King Alfred's locked shield wall decisively defeat Viking leader Guthrum?
  3. What happened under the peace treaty signed after Edington between King Alfred and Guthrum?
  4. How did King Alfred's network of 33 fortified "burhs" (such as Wareham and Wallingford) protect families across Wessex?
  5. What was the Alfred Jewel (inscribed "Alfred ordered me to be made"), and why did Alfred commission it?
Lesson 5: Life in Jorvik & the Danelaw — Were the Vikings Only Fierce Raiders? (c. AD 876–1000)
  1. Why did 40,000 wooden, leather, bone, and fabric objects survive underground beneath Coppergate in York (Viking Jorvik)?
  2. What does the York street name "Coppergate" actually mean in Old Norse — and what did archaeologists find on Source A (the Coppergate Helmet)?
  3. Which finds from Jorvik and Viking hoards prove that Viking trade networks reached the Middle East and the Red Sea?
  4. In Danelaw Viking society, who wore heavy iron household keys on their belts, could own land, and ran farms while husbands sailed?
  5. What was a Viking "Thing" (such as Tynwald Hill), and which modern English words come from Old Norse?
Lesson 6: Aethelflaed, Athelstan, Cnut & 1066 — Who Won the Struggle for England? (AD 900–1066)
  1. Which bold daughter of King Alfred ruled as "Lady of the Mercians" (AD 911–918), building burhs at Tamworth and Warwick and capturing Viking Derby and Leicester?
  2. Why do historians recognise King Athelstan (reigned AD 924–939) as the first true "King of All England"?
  3. What was "Danegeld," and how was Danish King Cnut's rule (AD 1016–1035) different from earlier raids?
  4. Why did a three-way crisis erupt over the English throne in January 1066?
  5. What happened at King Harold's TWO famous battles fought nineteen days apart in autumn 1066?

KEY STAGE 2 ILLUSTRATED GLOSSARY SYLLABLE HELPERS & DEFINITIONS

Historian's Word Bank (24 Essential Terms)

Clap the italic syllables out loud together to master tricky Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse words!

Migration Mi-gra-tion
Moving across land or sea from one country to make a permanent new home in another place.
Cyning Cy-ning
The Old English word for a warrior king who protected his people and rewarded loyal fighters in his mead hall.
Ceorl Ceorl
An ordinary free Anglo-Saxon farmer who ploughed fields, tended livestock, and owed service to his lord.
Mead Hall Mead Hall
A grand rectangular timber building with a central hearth fire where an Anglo-Saxon ruler feasted and held council.
Excavation Ex-ca-va-tion
Carefully digging and recording soil layers and buried artefacts to uncover clues about the past.
Grave Goods Grave Goods
Precious weapons, jewellery, coins, or vessels buried alongside a dead person for status or the afterlife.
Missionary Mis-sion-a-ry
A religious messenger sent to a new land to preach, teach, and persuade people to adopt a faith.
Monastery Mon-as-ter-y
A community of Christian monks or nuns dedicated to daily prayer, study, farming, and copying sacred books.
Scandinavia Scan-di-na-vi-a
The northern European homelands of the Vikings — modern Norway, Denmark, and Sweden.
Clinker-Built Clink-er-Built
Shipbuilding method overlapping flexible split oak planks (strakes) fastened with iron rivets and waterproofed with tarred wool.
Shallow Draught Shal-low Draught
Needing very little depth of water (barely 1 metre) to float, letting longships beach on sand or row far up inland rivers.
Monastery Reliquary Mon-as-ter-y Rel-i-qua-ry
A gold, silver, or jewelled casket kept inside a church to hold sacred saintly relics.
Fyrd Fyrd
An Anglo-Saxon part-time army of free local farmers and warriors summoned by their king whenever enemy invaders struck.
Shield wall Shield wall
A tight battlefield line where warriors stood shoulder-to-shoulder locking round wooden shields together like an unbroken fence.
Treaty Trea-ty
A formal written peace agreement sworn between rival rulers to end fighting and fix clear borders.
Danelaw Dane-law
The large area of northern and eastern England where Viking settlers lived and ruled under Danish laws after AD 878.
Jorvik Jor-vik
The bustling Viking capital, workshop centre, and river trading port captured in AD 866 — modern-day York.
Dirham Dir-ham
A pure silver coin minted in Islamic cities like Baghdad and Samarkand, traded along rivers by Viking merchants.
Knarr Knarr
A deep, wide-bellied Viking wooden cargo ship built to carry families, livestock, timber, and trade goods across oceans.
Thrall Thrall
An enslaved worker at the bottom of Viking society who had no freedom and carried out heavy farm or household labour.
Danegeld Dane-geld
Meaning "Dane-gold" — huge sums of silver pennies taxed from English families to pay Viking raiders to sail away.
Empire Em-pire
A group of several different countries or kingdoms ruled together under one powerful monarch, such as King Cnut's North Sea lands.
Witan Wi-tan
The Anglo-Saxon royal council of wise bishops and powerful earls who advised the king and chose the next monarch.
Heir Heir
The person — usually an eldest son, daughter, or close relative — who has the legal right to inherit the crown next.

MASTER CHRONOLOGICAL SPINE AD 410 TO OCTOBER 1066

10 Turning Points in the Making of England

AD 410–500
Angles, Saxons & Jutes Settle: After Roman legions leave, North Sea settlers build thatched timber halls and "-ham" / "-ton" farming villages.
c. AD 550–600
The Seven Kingdoms (Heptarchy): Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex compete for power across lowland Britain.
AD 597 & 635
Canterbury & Lindisfarne Missions: Augustine arrives from Rome in Kent (AD 597) and Aidan sails from Iona to Lindisfarne (AD 635), spreading Christianity.
c. AD 625
Sutton Hoo Royal Ship Burial: A 27-metre ship in Suffolk holds a dragon helmet, Sri Lankan garnets, and Byzantine silver—likely King Raedwald.
8 June AD 793
Viking Raid on Lindisfarne: Shallow-draught clinker longships strike St Cuthbert’s unguarded island monastery, opening the Viking Age.
AD 865–874
The Great Heathen Army: Ivar and Halfdan winter at camps like Repton and conquer Northumbria, East Anglia, and Mercia.
AD 878–886
Alfred the Great & The Danelaw: Alfred wins Edington, agrees the Watling Street Danelaw border with Guthrum, and builds 33 walled burhs.
c. AD 900
Global Trade in Viking Jorvik: Coppergate craftworkers carve antler combs and trade silk, amber, and Baghdad silver dirhams in York.
AD 917–1035
Aethelflaed, Athelstan & King Cnut: Aethelflaed and Athelstan unite all England (AD 927); later Danish King Cnut rules a peaceful North Sea Empire.
Sept–Oct 1066
Stamford Bridge to Hastings: Harold II defeats Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (25 Sept) before falling to William of Normandy at Hastings (14 Oct).
Big Picture Historian Discussion

1. Myth-Busting: How do Sutton Hoo's gold-and-garnet treasures AND York's 40,000 Coppergate finds smash old myths about "backward Dark Age Saxons" and "Vikings who only raided"?
2. Bridge to Year 7: On 14 October 1066 Duke William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings—how might Norman castles and French lords transform Anglo-Saxon England next?
